appSubtitle: Know your liver fibrosis risk from a routine blood test
introBody: LivrCheck calculates your FIB-4 score, a clinically validated estimate of liver fibrosis (scarring) risk, using four numbers from a standard blood test: your age, AST, ALT, and platelet count. These are part of a routine Liver Function Test (LFT) and Complete Blood Count (CBC).
notAlcoholBody: Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD) is caused by diet, obesity, diabetes, and sedentary lifestyle — not alcohol. Many Indian families assume a fatty liver diagnosis means an alcohol problem, which can delay proper diagnosis and care by years.
astHelp: Sometimes labeled SGOT on your report
altHelp: Sometimes labeled SGPT on your report
plateletsHelp: If your report shows lakhs/cmm (e.g. 2.5 lakh/cmm), multiply by 100 to get ×10⁹/L (e.g. 2.5 → 250).
diabetesLabel: Do you have diabetes or pre-diabetes?
familyHistoryLabel: Family history of fatty liver, cirrhosis, or metabolic syndrome?
tierLowExplanation: Your score suggests a low likelihood of advanced liver fibrosis (negative predictive value ~90.7%).
tierIntermediateExplanation: Your score is in an intermediate zone. This does not confirm fibrosis, but it cannot be ruled out either. Further evaluation is recommended.
tierHighExplanation: Your score is above the high-risk threshold (97% specificity for advanced fibrosis). This result should be taken seriously.
actionLow: Lifestyle counselling (diet, exercise, weight management). Repeat this test in 1–2 years.
actionIntermediate: Share this result with your GP or family doctor. A FibroScan may be recommended.
actionHigh: Please see a hepatologist or gastroenterologist soon. Bring this result and your original blood report.
bmiNote: Obesity and a high BMI are among the strongest known risk factors for NAFLD, independent of your FIB-4 score.
diabetesNote: Diabetes and pre-diabetes significantly increase both the risk of NAFLD and its progression. Regular monitoring matters.
familyHistoryNote: A family history of fatty liver or metabolic syndrome increases your own risk — worth mentioning to your doctor.
ageWarning: ⚠️ FIB-4 is validated primarily for adults aged 35–65. Outside this range the score is less reliable. Please discuss this result with a doctor.
disclaimerBody: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. FIB-4 is a statistical estimate based on published research. It does not measure liver fat (steatosis) — only fibrosis risk. Intermediate or High risk results require confirmation by a qualified medical professional. When in doubt, consult a doctor.
shareBody: NAFLD often runs in families — share LivrCheck with a relative.
shareMessage: I just checked my liver fibrosis risk using LivrCheck, a free app built from clinically validated research. Check yours too:
footerNote: LivrCheck is a free, open-source, non-commercial screening tool.

hm_greensWhy: Palak, methi and other greens are rich in fibre and antioxidants.
hm_greensKidsNote: Serve well cooked and mashed. Not for babies under 6 months.
hm_greensAdultNote: Part of the 300–400 g of vegetables advised daily.
hm_greensElderNote: Cook soft for easier chewing and digestion.
hm_greensBen1: Fibre and antioxidants help reduce fat build-up in the liver.
hm_greensBen2: Natural nitrates and folate help keep blood pressure in check.
hm_greensBen3: Iron and folate support healthy red blood cells.
hm_greensBen4: Vitamin K helps the body use calcium to keep bones strong.
hm_greensBen5: Lutein and zeaxanthin protect against cataract and age-related vision loss.
hm_greensBen6: Very low in calories and slow to digest, so blood sugar stays steady.
hm_greensRisk1: Palak is high in oxalate, which can form kidney stones in people prone to them.
hm_greensRisk2: Large, changing amounts of vitamin K can interfere with blood thinners such as warfarin.
hm_greensRisk3: Too much fibre at once can cause gas, bloating or loose motions.
hm_greensPrec1: Wash leaves thoroughly under running water to remove soil and pesticides.
hm_greensPrec2: Boil or blanch palak and throw away the water to cut oxalate.
hm_greensPrec3: Add lemon or amla to help the body absorb the iron.
hm_greensPrec4: Had kidney stones? Prefer methi or other greens, and ask your doctor.
hm_greensPrec5: On blood thinners? Keep the amount steady each day rather than stopping.
hm_greensPrec6: Do not reheat cooked greens many times, especially for small children.
hm_milletWhy: Ragi, jowar and bajra release energy slowly and help control sugar.
hm_milletKidsAmt: 1–2 small rotis or 1 katori ragi porridge a day
hm_milletKidsNote: Ragi porridge (ragi malt) is a traditional first food after 6 months.
hm_milletAdultAmt: Make at least half your daily grains whole grains
hm_milletAdultNote: For example, swap 2–3 of your usual rotis or rice portions for millets.
hm_milletElderNote: Soft porridge or upma is easier to chew and digest.
hm_milletBen1: Swapping refined grains for whole grains helps lower liver fat.
hm_milletBen2: Fibre slows digestion, so blood sugar rises gently after meals.
hm_milletBen3: Soluble fibre helps lower LDL ("bad") cholesterol.
hm_milletBen4: Ragi has about 3 times more calcium than milk, weight for weight.
hm_milletBen5: Bajra and ragi add iron to vegetarian diets.
hm_milletBen6: Fibre keeps digestion regular and feeds healthy gut bacteria.
hm_milletRisk1: Millets are still carbohydrates. Large portions can still raise blood sugar.
hm_milletRisk2: A sudden jump in fibre can cause gas and bloating.
hm_milletRisk3: Very large daily amounts of bajra may affect the thyroid when iodine intake is low.
hm_milletRisk4: Rich in potassium and phosphorus. People with kidney disease may need to limit them.
hm_milletPrec1: Switch gradually over 2–3 weeks and drink plenty of water.
hm_milletPrec2: Soak, sprout or ferment millets to help the body absorb iron and zinc.
hm_milletPrec3: Keep portions sensible: a millet roti still counts as a roti.
hm_milletPrec4: Use iodised salt if you eat bajra every day.
hm_milletPrec5: Packaged "multigrain" biscuits and snacks are often mostly maida. Read the label.
hm_milletPrec6: Have kidney disease? Ask your doctor how much is right for you.
hm_dalWhy: Good plant protein that keeps you full for longer.
hm_dalServing: 1 katori cooked dal (≈30 g raw masoor)
hm_dalKidsNote: Moong dal khichdi is gentle and easy to digest.
hm_dalAdultNote: Mix it up: dal, chana, rajma, sprouts. About 85 g raw pulses daily.
hm_dalElderNote: Well-cooked moong or masoor is easiest on the stomach.
hm_dalBen1: Plant protein instead of red and processed meat helps reduce liver fat.
hm_dalBen2: Fibre and potassium help lower cholesterol and blood pressure.
hm_dalBen3: Low glycaemic index, so blood sugar rises slowly.
hm_dalBen4: Protein helps keep muscles strong, especially after 60.
hm_dalBen5: A good source of iron and folate.
hm_dalRisk1: Natural sugars in pulses can cause gas and bloating.
hm_dalRisk2: High in protein, potassium and phosphorus. People with kidney disease may need to limit them.
hm_dalRisk3: A heavy ghee or butter tadka can double the calories.
hm_dalPrec1: Soak for 6–8 hours and throw away the water to reduce gas.
hm_dalPrec2: Never eat raw or undercooked rajma. It contains a toxin destroyed only by thorough boiling.
hm_dalPrec4: Add jeera, hing or ginger to help digestion.
hm_dalPrec5: Pair with rice or roti for complete protein.
hm_dalPrec6: Go easy on ghee and butter in the tadka.
hm_nutsWhy: A small handful a day adds healthy fats.
hm_nutsServing: 1 small handful, 30 g (≈15 almonds + 4 walnut halves)
hm_nutsKidsNote: Give powdered or finely chopped. Whole nuts can choke children under 5.
hm_nutsElderNote: Soaked or powdered nuts are easier to chew.
hm_nutsBen1: Vitamin E and omega-3 fats help protect the liver from fat damage.
hm_nutsBen2: Regular nut eaters have lower LDL cholesterol and fewer heart attacks.
hm_nutsBen3: Walnut omega-3s support brain health as you age.
hm_nutsBen4: Healthy fats and fibre improve how the body handles sugar.
hm_nutsRisk1: Nuts are calorie-dense. Two handfuls instead of one adds about 180 kcal.
hm_nutsRisk2: Large amounts can cause bloating or loose motions.
hm_nutsRisk3: Almonds contain oxalate, which can add to kidney stones in people prone to them.
hm_nutsRisk4: Tree nut allergy can cause severe reactions in some people.
hm_nutsPrec1: Portion out one handful instead of eating from the packet.
hm_nutsPrec2: Choose plain nuts. Avoid salted, sugar-coated or fried masala nuts.
hm_nutsPrec3: Soak almonds overnight if they are hard to digest.
hm_nutsPrec4: Throw away nuts that taste bitter or look mouldy. Mould (aflatoxin) damages the liver.
hm_nutsPrec5: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry place.
hm_nutsPrec6: Watch for signs of allergy the first time a child eats nuts.
hm_coffeeWhy: Linked with lower liver fibrosis risk — skip the sugar.
hm_coffeeServing: 1 cup (240 ml) brewed black coffee, no sugar
hm_coffeeKidsNote: Caffeine is not recommended for children.
hm_coffeeAdultNote: Up to 400 mg caffeine a day. If pregnant, no more than 200 mg (about 2 cups).
hm_coffeeElderNote: Have it before noon to protect sleep.
hm_coffeeBen1: Regular coffee drinkers have lower rates of liver scarring and cirrhosis.
hm_coffeeBen2: Studies link 2–3 cups a day with a lower risk of liver cancer.
hm_coffeeBen3: Long-term coffee drinking is linked with lower diabetes risk.
hm_coffeeBen4: Caffeine is linked with a lower risk of Parkinson's.
hm_coffeeRisk1: Too much causes poor sleep, anxiety and jitters.
hm_coffeeRisk2: Can cause palpitations and a short rise in blood pressure.
hm_coffeeRisk3: Can worsen acidity and reflux, especially on an empty stomach.
hm_coffeeRisk4: Very high intake slightly reduces calcium absorption.
hm_coffeePrec1: Skip the sugar and cream. Sugar adds liver fat and cancels the benefit.
hm_coffeePrec3: Have it after breakfast if you get acidity.
hm_coffeePrec4: Paper-filtered coffee is better for cholesterol than boiled, unfiltered coffee.
hm_coffeePrec5: Pregnant? Keep to 2 cups or fewer a day.
hm_coffeePrec6: Have heart rhythm problems or high BP? Ask your doctor first.
hm_drinksWhy: Soft drinks and packaged juices add fructose, which builds liver fat.
hm_drinksKidsNote: One can has more sugar than a child should have in a whole day.
hm_drinksAdultAmt: Best avoided; an occasional small glass at most
hm_drinksAdultNote: WHO advises under 25 g (6 tsp) of added sugar a day from all foods.
hm_drinksElderNote: Choose water, chaas or unsweetened nimbu pani.
hm_drinksBen1: For people on diabetes medicines, a small glass of juice can quickly correct a sugar low.
hm_drinksRisk1: The liver turns fructose straight into fat. Sugary drinks are a leading cause of fatty liver.
hm_drinksRisk2: Daily sugary drinks raise the risk of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes.
hm_drinksRisk4: Sugar and acid together cause tooth decay.
hm_drinksRisk5: Liquid calories don't fill you up, so they add weight quickly.
hm_drinksSwap1Body: Fresh lime water with a pinch of salt. No sugar, or very little.
hm_drinksSwap2Body: Cooling, with protein and gut-friendly bacteria.
hm_drinksSwap3Body: Natural electrolytes. Have one glass, not several.
hm_drinksSwap4Body: Eat the orange instead of drinking the juice. The fibre slows the sugar.
hm_drinksPrec1: "Fruit drink" and "nectar" usually mean added sugar. Read the label.
hm_drinksPrec2: Even 100% fruit juice is high in sugar. Keep to one small glass.
hm_drinksPrec3: More than 5 g sugar per 100 ml is high.
hm_drinksPrec4: Diet sodas avoid sugar, but plain water is still the best choice.
hm_drinksPrec5: Don't give sugary drinks to children.
hm_friedWhy: Samosas, pakoras and chips are high in unhealthy fats.
hm_friedKidsAmt: An occasional treat, once a week at most
hm_friedKidsNote: Keep it to a small portion.
hm_friedElderNote: Heavy to digest. Best avoided with heart disease or high BP.
hm_friedRisk1: Extra calories and saturated fats build up as liver fat.
hm_friedRisk2: Trans fats from reused oil raise bad cholesterol and lower good cholesterol.
hm_friedRisk4: Oily food often triggers acidity and indigestion.
hm_friedRisk5: One samosa is about the calories of two rotis with dal.
hm_friedSwap1Body: Crunchy, high in protein and fibre.
hm_friedSwap2Body: Light and low in fat. Roast with a little ghee and spices.
hm_friedSwap3Body: Tangy and filling, with lots of fibre.
hm_friedSwap4Body: Dhokla, idli or momos (steamed, not fried).
hm_friedPrec1: Avoid street snacks fried in dark, reused oil.
hm_friedPrec2: At home, don't reuse frying oil more than 2–3 times (FSSAI advice).
hm_friedPrec3: Try an air fryer or oven for samosas and pakoras.
hm_friedPrec4: Eat with mint chutney and salad instead of ketchup.
hm_friedPrec5: Stick to one piece and eat it slowly.
hm_maidaWhy: White bread, biscuits and bakery items spike blood sugar.
hm_maidaKidsNote: Choose whole-wheat bread and home-made snacks instead.
hm_maidaAdultNote: Swap for whole grains most days.
hm_maidaElderNote: Soft whole-wheat options are just as easy to chew.
hm_maidaBen1: Plain toast is gentle on the stomach when recovering from loose motions or vomiting.
hm_maidaRisk1: Quick sugar spikes push the liver to store more fat.
hm_maidaRisk2: Digests almost like sugar, raising the risk of type 2 diabetes.
hm_maidaRisk3: Very little fibre, which can lead to constipation.
hm_maidaRisk4: Raises triglycerides, a type of fat in the blood.
hm_maidaRisk5: Leaves you hungry again soon, so you eat more.
hm_maidaSwap1Body: Atta keeps the bran and fibre that maida loses.
hm_maidaSwap2Body: Check that "whole wheat" is the first ingredient.
hm_maidaSwap3Body: Millets add fibre, calcium and iron.
hm_maidaSwap4Body: A filling breakfast that releases energy slowly.
hm_maidaPrec1: "Wheat flour" or "refined wheat flour" on a label means maida.
hm_maidaPrec2: "Brown bread" is often coloured maida. Look for "100% whole wheat".
hm_maidaPrec3: Bakery items, naan and pizza bases are mostly maida, and often high in fat and sugar too.
hm_maidaPrec4: Pair any bread with protein or vegetables to slow the sugar rise.
hm_maidaPrec5: Cut down on biscuits and rusks with tea.
hm_tip1Body: Brisk walking 5 days a week reduces liver fat, even without weight loss.
hm_tip2Body: If you are overweight, losing 7–10% of body weight can reverse fatty liver.
hm_tip3Body: Poor sleep is linked to weight gain and insulin resistance.
hm_tip4Body: Get HbA1c tested once a year — diabetes speeds up liver damage.
hm_tip5Body: Some painkillers and herbal supplements can harm the liver. Ask your doctor first.
hm_faq1A: Fatty liver means extra fat has built up in liver cells. The most common type, NAFLD (now also called MASLD), is linked to diet, weight and diabetes — not alcohol.
hm_faq2A: Yes. In its early stages, fatty liver can often be reversed with weight loss, a healthier diet and regular exercise.
hm_faq3Q: I am not overweight. Can I still have fatty liver?
hm_faq3A: Yes. "Lean" fatty liver is common in South Asians, who can store fat around the organs even at a normal weight.
hm_faq4Q: What does my FIB-4 score mean?
hm_faq4A: FIB-4 estimates the chance of liver scarring (fibrosis) from four blood test values. It is a screening tool, not a diagnosis.
hm_faq5A: Start with your family doctor. For an intermediate or high score, they may refer you to a gastroenterologist or hepatologist.
hm_faq6A: An ultrasound can show liver fat. A FibroScan measures liver stiffness to check for scarring.

pp_collectBody: Account details (email, name). Profile details you enter (age, gender, height, weight, language). Your health check answers and results, blood test values if you enter them, and your daily logs (water, food, exercise, steps, sleep). Coins and streaks you earn.
pp_whyBody: To calculate and show your results, track your progress over time, personalise your daily goals and run the coin rewards. We do not use it for advertising and we never sell it.
pp_whereBody: On secure servers run by our database provider (Supabase). Every record is protected so that only your account can read it.
pp_whoBody: Only you. Our team does not look at individual records except to fix a problem you report, or where the law requires it.
pp_keepBody: For as long as you have an account. When you delete your account, all your data is deleted straight away.
pp_rightsBody: You can see and edit your profile in the app at any time, and delete your account and all your data yourself (Profile → Delete my account) — it is erased immediately. For a copy of your data or any other request, email {email}.
pp_medicalBody: LivrCheck is a screening and wellness tool. It does not diagnose any condition. Always talk to a doctor about your health.
pp_changesBody: If this policy changes we will ask you to agree again in the app.
sv_labNeedAllThree: FIB-4 needs all three numbers. Without them, your results won't include it.
gd_heroSub: Know your liver, protect your health
gd_heroBody: A guide for children, adults, older adults and families.
gd_disclaimer: This guide gives general health information and is not a substitute for professional medical advice. Pediatric assessment differs from adult assessment (e.g., test ranges and follow-up plans can be different).
gd_reviewed: This guidebook has been reviewed by a multidisciplinary team of healthcare professionals (e.g., hepatology, pediatrics, family medicine and nutrition).
gd_homeCardBody: Know your liver, your risk, the tests and what you can do — for every age.
gd_ckNone: Nothing ticked. Keep up your healthy habits and check again if anything changes.
gd_ckResult: You ticked {n} of {total}. If you have concerns, ask a healthcare professional whether liver assessment is appropriate.
gd_chTapHint: Pick a day, then tick each habit you did.
gd_c1B: How the liver works, what it does for your body, and why it matters for your overall health.
gd_c2B: The factors that can increase your risk of fatty liver and related liver problems.
gd_c3B: Tests and assessments: what they involve, what the results may mean, and when to get checked.
gd_c4B: Improve your liver health through food, physical activity, sleep, weight and medicines (if needed).
gd_c5B: Set goals, track your progress and keep a healthier liver over time.
gd_c6B: Who to see, and trusted sources for more information.
gd_lmIntro: Your liver is one of the most important organs in your body, carrying out many essential functions to keep you healthy.
gd_lm1B: Converts food into useful substances and stores excess nutrients (such as glucose and vitamins).
gd_lm2B: Keeps your energy levels balanced by storing and releasing glucose when needed.
gd_lm3B: Makes bile, a fluid that helps to digest and absorb fats and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K).
gd_lm4B: Breaks down and helps remove waste products, toxins, alcohol and medicines from the body.
gd_lm5B: Stores important substances, such as vitamins (A, D, E, K and B12) and minerals (such as iron and copper), for when the body needs them.
gd_lm6B: Makes proteins that help with blood clotting, maintain fluid balance and support the immune system.
gd_lmC: The liver supports growth and development.
gd_lmA: The liver supports energy and metabolic functions.
gd_lmO: The liver remains important for nutrition, metabolism and medicine processing.
gd_lmKey: Your liver works continuously, often without you noticing.
gd_flIntro: Fatty liver disease (also called hepatic steatosis) means that excess fat builds up in the liver, mainly as fat droplets inside liver cells, which can affect the liver's structure and function.
gd_flNormalB: A small amount of fat in the liver (usually less than 5% of liver weight) is normal. When fat exceeds this level, it is considered fatty liver disease.
gd_flGoodB: A healthy liver contains a small amount of fat and has a normal structure and function.
gd_flGood1: Only a small amount of fat (usually < 5%)
gd_flGood3: Carries out all its important roles
gd_flBadB: Excess fat builds up inside liver cells, as fat droplets. Over time, this can make the liver enlarged and yellowish and can affect its function.
gd_flBad1: Excess fat accumulated inside liver cells
gd_flBad2: May make the liver enlarged and yellowish
gd_flBad3: Can affect liver function over time
gd_flBad4: Often does not cause noticeable symptoms
gd_flC: Liver fat can occur in children, including those who are not overweight.
gd_flA: Liver fat can occur in adults, including people who appear to have a healthy body weight.
gd_flO: Liver fat can also occur in older adults, and it may be more common with age, even in those who are not overweight.
gd_flKey: Globally, about 1 in 4 adults (around 25%) has fatty liver disease.
gd_flSrc: Source: Younossi ZM, et al. Hepatology. 2016;64(1):73–84.
gd_tyT: Main types of fatty liver disease
gd_tyWhyB: Fatty liver disease is not a single condition. The type is important because the causes, risk of progression, monitoring and treatment approach can be different.
gd_ty1B: The most common type. It is linked to metabolic risk factors such as being overweight or having Type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure or abnormal cholesterol.
gd_ty1N: Caused by metabolic factors (not related to excess alcohol).
gd_ty2B: A more serious form of MASLD. It involves fat in the liver along with inflammation and liver cell damage, which can lead to fibrosis (scarring) and, in some people, cirrhosis.
gd_ty2N: A progressive form that can cause liver scarring over time.
gd_ty3B: Caused by regular or long-term heavy alcohol use, which can lead to fat accumulation, inflammation, liver cell damage and scarring.
gd_ty3N: Related to regular or heavy alcohol use.
gd_ty4T: MetALD (metabolic dysfunction and alcohol-associated liver disease)
gd_ty4B: Occurs in people who have metabolic risk factors (such as obesity, Type 2 diabetes or high cholesterol) and also consume moderate-to-heavy amounts of alcohol.
gd_ty4N: Involves both metabolic risk factors and alcohol use.
gd_tyC: Pediatric assessment and causes require special consideration.
gd_tyA: Metabolic risk factors and alcohol history are important.
gd_tyO: Metabolic conditions, alcohol exposure, medicines and other causes may coexist.
gd_tyKey: A healthcare professional determines the diagnosis.
gd_stIntro: Fatty liver disease can range from a build-up of fat in the liver to inflammation, scarring (fibrosis) and, in some people, cirrhosis. It may progress over time, remain stable or even improve with the right changes and care.
gd_st1B: Excess fat builds up in liver cells (fat droplets), usually without noticeable symptoms.
gd_st2B: Fat build-up with inflammation and liver cell injury. This can lead to scarring over time.
gd_st3B: A build-up of scar tissue (fibrosis) in the liver, often from ongoing inflammation and liver cell injury.
gd_st4B: Extensive scarring that changes the liver's structure and can reduce its function.
gd_stDiffT: MASH and fibrosis are related but different
gd_stDiff1: MASH (steatohepatitis) means fat build-up with inflammation and liver cell injury.
gd_stDiff2: Fibrosis means the build-up of scar tissue in the liver, which can occur after ongoing inflammation (such as in MASH).
gd_stSeqT: The disease does not always progress in a fixed sequence
gd_stSeq1: Some people may stay at the steatosis stage for many years.
gd_stSeq2: Some may develop MASH and fibrosis.
gd_stSeq3: Progression to cirrhosis occurs in a smaller number of people.
gd_stSeq4: With appropriate care, the disease can sometimes be stabilized or even reversed (especially in the earlier stages).
gd_stAll: Advanced liver disease can occur across age groups, including children, adults and older adults, although the causes and evaluation may differ.
gd_stKey: Early assessment can help identify risk and guide care.
gd_rkIntro: Fatty liver can occur in people with excess body weight, but it can also occur in people with a healthy-looking body weight (lean fatty liver).
gd_rkC2B: e.g., higher blood sugar, cholesterol or triglycerides
gd_rkC4B: e.g., short or poor quality sleep
gd_rkO4B: e.g., thyroid disease, chronic kidney disease
gd_rkLeanB: Fatty liver can occur even in people who are not overweight. It is often linked to metabolic risk factors such as diabetes, high blood pressure or abnormal cholesterol.
gd_rkSaB: People of South Asian ethnicity can develop fatty liver at lower levels of body weight and waist size. Screening considerations for Asian adults:
gd_rkKey: Body shape alone cannot tell you whether your liver is healthy.
gd_ckIntro: Use this quick checklist to reflect on factors that can be linked to fatty liver disease. It is for awareness only and does not replace a medical assessment or diagnosis.
gd_ckC1: Is there a family history of fatty liver, diabetes or other metabolic conditions?
gd_ckC2: Has your child been diagnosed with a metabolic condition (e.g., overweight/obesity, high cholesterol or Type 2 diabetes)?
gd_ckC3: Is your child usually less active (e.g., little physical activity or lots of screen time)?
gd_ckC4: Does your child often have sleep problems (e.g., snoring or poor sleep)?
gd_ckC5: Has your child ever had a liver-related concern or abnormal liver test result?
gd_ckCNote: A parent or caregiver can help complete this checklist.
gd_ckA1: Have you been diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes?
gd_ckA2: Do you have high cholesterol or triglycerides?
gd_ckA3: Do you have high blood pressure?
gd_ckA4: Do you have increased abdominal fat (a larger waist size)?
gd_ckA5: Do you drink alcohol regularly or in moderate to large amounts?
gd_ckA6: Have you ever had abnormal liver test results or been told you have a fatty liver?
gd_ckO1: Do you have any metabolic conditions (e.g., Type 2 diabetes, high cholesterol or high blood pressure)?
gd_ckO2: Have you previously been told you have a fatty liver or had abnormal liver test or imaging results?
gd_ckO3: Do you take medicines that could affect the liver (e.g., long-term or multiple medicines)?
gd_ckO4: Do you drink alcohol regularly or in moderate to large amounts?
gd_ckO5: Do you have other long-term illnesses (e.g., kidney disease, heart disease or thyroid disease)?
gd_ckKey: If you have concerns, ask a healthcare professional whether liver assessment is appropriate.
gd_syT: Fatty liver often causes no symptoms
gd_syIntro: Many people only find out they have it during routine blood tests or an ultrasound done for another reason.
gd_syEarlyB: If symptoms do appear, they are often vague and can be mistaken for other conditions.
gd_sy1B: Feeling unusually tired or lacking energy without an obvious cause.
gd_sy2B: A dull ache, fullness or heaviness in the upper right side of the belly (where the liver sits).
gd_sy3B: Simply feeling unwell or experiencing mild, unexplained weakness.
gd_syLateB: If the liver develops severe inflammation or scarring, the body may show clearer signs that the liver is struggling to function.
gd_sy4B: Yellowing of the skin and the whites of the eyes.
gd_sy5B: Swelling in the legs, ankles or feet, and a tightly bloated abdomen due to fluid build-up.
gd_syC1: Symptoms, if present, are often mild and non-specific (e.g., tiredness or abdominal discomfort).
gd_syC2: A healthcare professional should evaluate any persistent or concerning symptoms.
gd_syA1: Symptoms can be vague (e.g., fatigue or upper abdominal discomfort) or may be absent.
gd_syA2: Persistent symptoms should be assessed by a healthcare professional.
gd_syO1: Symptoms may be subtle (e.g., reduced appetite, fatigue or abdominal fullness) and can overlap with other conditions.
gd_syO2: Ongoing or new symptoms should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.
gd_syWeightT: See a doctor: unexplained weight loss
gd_syWeightB: Dropping weight without trying can be a sign of more advanced liver disease or another medical problem and should be checked by a healthcare professional.
gd_drIntro: Fatty liver disease often has no symptoms, but it is important to get medical advice if you have risk factors, abnormal test results or any concerning signs.
gd_dr1B: e.g., ongoing fatigue, abdominal discomfort or reduced appetite.
gd_dr2B: e.g., elevated liver enzymes, or imaging findings such as fatty liver on ultrasound.
gd_dr3B: e.g., Type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, excess abdominal fat or regular alcohol use.
gd_dr4B: e.g., persistent tiredness, unintentional weight loss or feeling generally unwell.
gd_drUrgentT: Seek urgent care (e.g., at an emergency department) if you have:
gd_dr6B: Which can be a sign of bleeding in the digestive tract.
gd_dr7B: e.g., marked drowsiness, difficulty staying awake or not knowing where you are.
gd_dr8B: e.g., from the mouth or nose, or bruising easily with large or frequent bruises.
gd_dr9B: e.g., increasing abdominal swelling, breathing difficulty or severe weakness.
gd_drC1: Involve a parent or caregiver in noticing concerns and deciding whether to seek medical advice.
gd_drC2: A healthcare professional can assess symptoms, risk factors and any relevant test results.
gd_drA1: Seek a medical assessment if you have persistent concerns, abnormal test results, known risk factors or unexplained symptoms.
gd_drA2: Discuss your lifestyle, medical history and alcohol use with a healthcare professional.
gd_drO1: Seek medical advice if you have new or persistent concerns, abnormal test results or a known risk of liver disease.
gd_drO2: Review all your medical conditions and medicines (including long-term or multiple medicines) with a healthcare professional, as these may affect your liver.
gd_drKey: Do not wait for symptoms before discussing relevant risk factors.
gd_dtIntro: Fatty liver often does not cause noticeable symptoms, especially in its early stages. It is usually detected through a combination of your medical history, examination, blood tests and imaging, which help confirm the condition and assess its severity.
gd_dt1B: Review your lifestyle, medical conditions (e.g., diabetes, high cholesterol) and alcohol use.
gd_dt2B: Check your weight, calculate your BMI and examine your abdomen to look for signs of an enlarged liver.
gd_dt3B: Assess liver function (e.g., ALT, AST) and metabolic factors (e.g., blood sugar, cholesterol, triglycerides).
gd_dt4B: An ultrasound (usually first-line) and, when needed, tests of liver stiffness (e.g., FibroScan/MRE) or other imaging (e.g., CT or MRI).
gd_dtC1B: Review family history, growth and lifestyle (e.g., diet, activity and screen time).
gd_dtC2B: Check growth, weight status (e.g., BMI-for-age) and overall development.
gd_dtC3B: Age-appropriate blood tests (e.g., liver function and metabolic tests) if fatty liver is suspected.
gd_dtA1B: Evaluate metabolic risk factors (e.g., Type 2 diabetes, abdominal adiposity, high blood pressure and high cholesterol).
gd_dtA2B: Check liver enzymes (e.g., ALT, AST) and other relevant blood tests.
gd_dtA3B: Estimate the risk of liver scarring (fibrosis) using non-invasive tools (e.g., blood-based scores and/or elastography).
gd_dtO3B: Review other medical conditions and all current medicines, as they may affect the liver. Consider age-related factors (e.g., changes in test results or imaging interpretation).
gd_dtKey: No single test answers every question about liver health.
gd_f4Intro: FIB-4 (Fibrosis-4 Index) is a non-invasive, widely used initial risk-stratification score that estimates the likelihood of significant liver scarring (fibrosis) in appropriate adult patients.
gd_f4LowB: Advanced fibrosis is unlikely. Routine monitoring is usually appropriate.
gd_f4MidB: The risk is uncertain. Consider additional fibrosis assessment (e.g., transient elastography).
gd_f4HighB: A higher likelihood of significant fibrosis. Additional assessment and specialist evaluation are recommended.
gd_f4C: FIB-4 is not recommended as a routine pediatric fibrosis assessment tool.
gd_f4A: FIB-4 can help determine whether additional fibrosis assessment is needed.
gd_f4O: Interpretation requires age-adjusted considerations and clinical judgment.
gd_f4LimB: FIB-4 is less reliable in adults younger than 35 years and older than 65 years, and results should always be interpreted in the context of the overall clinical picture.
gd_f4Key: You can work out your FIB-4 in the Check tab by adding your blood report values.
gd_tsIntro: Different tests give different information about your liver. Results need to be interpreted by a healthcare professional together with your medical history, examination and overall risk factors.
gd_ts1B: Signs of liver cell injury or inflammation.
gd_ts1N: Can be normal even when significant scarring (fibrosis) is present.
gd_ts2B: Conditions often linked to fatty liver.
gd_ts2N: Do not diagnose fatty liver or measure liver damage.
gd_ts3B: Detects a fatty liver and looks for other liver problems.
gd_ts3N: Less sensitive for mild fat and cannot reliably assess scarring.
gd_ts4N: Results can be affected by factors such as inflammation or high body weight.
gd_ts5B: Estimates the amount of fat in the liver.
gd_ts5N: Estimates fat rather than providing a direct measurement.
gd_ts6B: Accurately measures the amount of liver fat.
gd_ts6N: More costly and not usually needed for routine assessment.
gd_ts7B: Examines liver tissue to confirm inflammation, fat and scarring.
gd_ts7N: Invasive, with a small risk of bleeding or other complications.
gd_tsC: Test selection and interpretation are based on individual risk factors and growth and development.
gd_tsA: A combination of blood tests and imaging (e.g., ultrasound or FibroScan) is often used, with results interpreted together with your risk factors.
gd_tsO: Test selection and interpretation may be adjusted for other health conditions and medicines.
gd_tsKey: Normal liver enzymes do not always exclude significant liver disease.
gd_afIntro: The next step depends on your overall risk of liver disease, which is based on your test results, risk factors, other health conditions and age. This helps ensure you get the right follow-up and care.
gd_afC3B: e.g., concerns about liver scarring or ongoing liver problems
gd_afA3T: Monitoring or specialist referral based on results
gd_afA3B: e.g., routine follow-up for low risk, or referral for signs of significant liver disease
gd_afO1T: Adult fibrosis pathway with age-adjusted interpretation
gd_afO2B: e.g., FibroScan, ultrasound or other tests, as needed
gd_afO3B: e.g., monitoring, lifestyle support and treatment of other health conditions, with specialist input when needed
gd_afAsk1: What do my test results mean for my liver health?
gd_afAsk2: Do I need any additional tests?
gd_afAsk3: How often should I be monitored?
gd_afAsk4: Do I need to see a liver specialist?
gd_afAsk5: What can I do now to lower my risk and protect my liver?
gd_afSpecT: Why might I need specialist evaluation?
gd_afSpecB: A specialist (e.g., a liver doctor or hepatologist) can provide a more detailed evaluation, confirm the diagnosis, assess the stage of liver disease and recommend a personalized management plan if your risk is higher or your test results are concerning.
gd_fuIntro: Follow-up helps track your liver health over time, check for changes, and decide if additional tests or treatment are needed. The plan is personalized based on your age, risk factors and test results.
gd_fuCWhat: Liver enzymes (ALT, AST); metabolic factors (e.g., weight, blood sugar, cholesterol); liver imaging (e.g., ultrasound), if needed.
gd_fuCWhen: Based on the underlying condition, risk factors and initial results. The timing is individualized (e.g., during routine follow-up visits or sooner if concerns arise).
gd_fuAWhat: Liver enzymes (ALT, AST); metabolic factors (e.g., blood sugar, cholesterol); liver fibrosis risk (e.g., FIB-4); liver imaging (e.g., ultrasound, FibroScan), if indicated.
gd_fuAWho: Primary care provider or liver specialist (hepatologist).
gd_fuAWhen: If FIB-4 is used and results are non-high risk, guideline-based reassessment is typically every 2–3 years (lower risk) or every 1–2 years (higher risk within the non-high range). Sooner reassessment may be needed if your health status changes or risk increases.
gd_fuOWhat: Liver enzymes (ALT, AST); metabolic factors (e.g., blood sugar, cholesterol); liver fibrosis risk (e.g., FIB-4, with age-adjusted interpretation); liver imaging (e.g., ultrasound, FibroScan), if indicated.
gd_fuOWho: Primary care provider or liver specialist (hepatologist).
gd_fuOWhen: Typically every 1–2 years, depending on overall risk, other health conditions and prior results. Sooner reassessment may be needed if there are changes in symptoms, test results or clinical status.
gd_fuRecB: Soon you'll be able to save each test here — date, test, result and next appointment — and get a reminder before it's due.
gd_fuKey: Cirrhosis and other advanced conditions need different surveillance plans.
gd_fdKeyTop: Eating well supports liver and metabolic health.
gd_fd1B: A variety of colourful vegetables (e.g., spinach, cauliflower, carrot, beans).
gd_fd2B: Whole, less-processed grains (e.g., whole wheat roti, brown rice, millets).
gd_fd3B: Healthy protein sources (e.g., dal, beans, lentils, paneer, fish, chicken, eggs, soy).
gd_fdIndT: Indian examples for a liver-friendly meal
gd_fdC1: Choose nutritious meals that support growth and development.
gd_fdC2: Avoid restrictive dieting (e.g., very low-calorie diets) unless advised by a healthcare professional.
gd_fdA1: Aim for balanced meals with a variety of nutrient-rich foods.
gd_fdA2: Include fibre (e.g., whole grains, vegetables, fruits) and healthy fats (e.g., nuts, seeds, vegetable oils).
gd_fdA3: Choose appropriate portion sizes to help maintain a healthy weight.
gd_fdO1: Ensure adequate nutrition and protein (e.g., dal, paneer, eggs, fish, chicken, legumes).
gd_fdO2: Adjust food choices based on individual medical needs (e.g., diabetes, heart or kidney conditions), with guidance from a healthcare professional.
gd_fdKey: Stay well-hydrated throughout the day (e.g., with water, unsweetened tea or buttermilk).
gd_ltIntro: Some foods and drinks add extra sugar, unhealthy fats and calories, which may increase the risk of fatty liver and other liver and metabolic problems. Have them less often and choose healthier, everyday options.
gd_lt2B: e.g., fruit drinks with added sugar
gd_lt4B: e.g., burgers, instant noodles, ready-to-eat meals
gd_lt4sB: e.g., roti, dal, vegetables, salad and curd
gd_ltC1: Choose water, milk or unsweetened drinks.
gd_ltC2: Keep high-sugar drinks and fried or packaged snacks for occasional treats.
gd_ltA1: Maintain regular meal times and avoid frequent high-calorie snacks.
gd_ltA2: Limit foods high in added sugar, refined grains and unhealthy fats.
gd_ltO1: Ensure adequate and balanced nutrition, including enough protein.
gd_ltO2: Choose easier-to-digest, nutrient-rich options as needed (e.g., dal, eggs, curd, soft-cooked vegetables).
gd_ltKey: Small, realistic changes matter more than perfection.
gd_acIntro: Being active helps reduce excess body fat, improve metabolism, and lower the risk of fatty liver and other liver problems.
gd_acC2T: At least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity daily
gd_acA3T: Plus muscle-strengthening activities on at least 2 days a week
gd_acO2T: At least 150 minutes per week (as tolerated)
gd_acO3T: Plus balance and strength exercises on at least 2 days a week
gd_acSafeB: Adapt the type, intensity and duration of activity to your own ability, including if you have a disability, frailty or a medical condition. Ask your healthcare professional for personalized advice.
gd_acSrc1: World Health Organization. WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour. 2020.
gd_acSrc2: Keating SE, et al. Exercise for non-alcoholic fatty liver disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Hepatol. 2022;77:667–682.
gd_slIntro: Sleep and daily routines support overall metabolic health, including healthier weight, blood sugar and liver health.
gd_slC3B: e.g., a consistent bedtime and wake-up time
gd_slA1B: e.g., similar bedtime and wake-up time most days
gd_slA2T: Take movement breaks during long periods of sitting
gd_slA3T: Be alert to possible sleep apnoea signs
gd_slA3B: e.g., loud snoring, pauses in breathing, daytime tiredness — and discuss them with a clinician
gd_slO1B: e.g., similar bedtime and wake-up time
gd_slO2B: e.g., walking, light exercises or daily activities
gd_slO3T: Discuss persistent sleep difficulties with a clinician
gd_slO3B: e.g., trouble falling asleep, frequent waking or excessive daytime sleepiness
gd_slHabT: Healthy daily habits for better sleep and metabolic health
gd_slHab3: Keep a consistent routine (e.g., sleep, meals and activity times).
gd_slChB: For the next 7 days, try to: (1) keep a consistent bedtime and wake-up time, (2) limit recreational screen time in the evening, and (3) be active during the day. Notice how you feel at the end of the week.
gd_wtIntro: Healthy body composition and nutrition matter for liver and metabolic health, but the goals can be different at each stage of life.
gd_wtC1: Focus on healthy growth and development.
gd_wtC3: Support regular physical activity and active play.
gd_wtC4: Have growth, nutrition and overall health checked by a pediatrician.
gd_wtA1: Aim for a medically appropriate weight-management goal with guidance from a healthcare professional.
gd_wtA2: A suitable, sustained reduction in body weight can reduce fat in the liver, lower inflammation, and slow or improve liver scarring (fibrosis).
gd_wtO1: Focus on preserving muscle strength and function.
gd_wtO2: Ensure adequate protein intake (e.g., dal, eggs, curd, milk, legumes).
gd_wtO3: Help prevent frailty by staying active and well nourished.
gd_wtO4: Use a careful, individualized approach to weight management, considering overall health, medical conditions and medicines.
gd_wtCrashB: Restrictive diets can be unhealthy and may lead to nutrient deficiencies, loss of muscle and other problems. They can be especially harmful to growing children and frail older adults.
gd_mbIntro: Metabolic health and liver health are closely linked. Diabetes, abnormal cholesterol or triglycerides and high blood pressure can increase fat in the liver and, over time, raise the risk of liver inflammation, scarring (fibrosis) and other liver problems.
gd_mb1B: Higher blood sugar can be linked to more liver fat and a greater risk of liver inflammation and scarring. Keep blood sugar under control, as advised by your healthcare professional.
gd_mb2B: Higher triglycerides and an unhealthy cholesterol pattern can increase liver fat and the risk of liver disease. Improve and keep healthy lipid levels through a balanced lifestyle and, if needed, medicines as advised by your clinician.
gd_mb3B: High blood pressure often occurs with other metabolic conditions (e.g., overweight, diabetes) and can be part of a higher overall risk for liver and heart health. Keep blood pressure within your target range, with lifestyle measures and treatment as advised by your healthcare professional.
gd_mbC: Pediatric diagnosis and targets differ from adult targets. See a pediatric healthcare professional for age-appropriate assessment and management.
gd_mbA: Metabolic conditions such as diabetes, high cholesterol/triglycerides and high blood pressure should be managed with individualized clinical goals.
gd_mbO: Targets may need adjusting for frailty, other illnesses and treatment risks (e.g., risk of low blood sugar or side effects).
gd_mdIntro: Treatment depends on the cause, disease stage, age and other health conditions.
gd_md1B: Healthy, balanced diet and portion control · regular physical activity · weight management (as appropriate) · avoiding alcohol and limiting processed foods.
gd_md2B: Manage diabetes (maintain target control) · control cholesterol and triglycerides (as per guidelines) · keep blood pressure within target range.
gd_md3T: Medicines for selected patients with MASH
gd_md3B: Considered for patients with more advanced disease or higher risk. The choice of medicine depends on individual factors (e.g., disease stage, other conditions, potential benefits and risks).
gd_mdC2: Do not extrapolate adult drug approvals.
gd_mdA: Some medicines may be appropriate for specific patients, depending on approved indications and availability.
gd_mdO: Treatment decisions must consider other medicines, organ function and tolerability.
gd_mdSelfB: Avoid self-medication and unverified herbal products.
gd_chIntro: Small, consistent changes can make a big difference for your liver. Tick each habit when you complete it. You can repeat this plan every week and keep adding new goals.
gd_ch1B: Aim for 6–8 glasses (1.5–2 litres) throughout the day.
gd_ch2B: Include vegetables in at least two meals.
gd_ch3B: Choose fresh fruits instead of fruit juices or sweets.
gd_ch4B: Limit fried foods, sugary drinks, packaged snacks and ultra-processed foods.
gd_ch5B: Aim for at least 30 minutes of moderate activity (e.g., walking, cycling, yoga).
gd_ch6B: Take short movement breaks every 1–2 hours.
gd_ch7B: Aim for 7–8 hours of good quality sleep.
gd_ch8B: Take your medicines as advised for diabetes, cholesterol, blood pressure or other conditions.
gd_chSuccessH: What went well? (e.g., walked daily, ate more vegetables, drank water, slept better)
gd_chImproveT: One thing I want to improve next week
gd_chImproveH: What will I focus on? (e.g., fewer sugary drinks, more activity, earlier sleep, taking medicines regularly)
gd_rememberB: You do not have to be perfect. Even small steps can improve your liver health over time. If you have any medical conditions, follow your doctor's advice.
gd_plIntro: Small, consistent changes can make a big difference for your liver. Use this plan to set realistic goals, build healthy habits and take steps towards a healthier liver.
gd_pl1H: What do I want to achieve for my liver health? (e.g., lose weight, reduce sugar, stop alcohol, improve fitness)
gd_pl2T: 2. One food change I will make
gd_pl2H: Be specific (e.g., add one extra serving of vegetables daily, replace sugary drinks with water, include whole grains).
gd_pl3T: 3. One activity change I will start or increase
gd_pl3H: Be specific (e.g., walk for 30 minutes, do yoga, use the stairs instead of the lift).
gd_pl4T: 4. One habit I will reduce or avoid
gd_pl4H: Be specific (e.g., avoid alcohol, limit junk food, reduce sitting time).
gd_pl5H: When will I check my progress or meet my healthcare provider? (e.g., date for blood tests, doctor appointment)
gd_pl5Ask: I will ask my healthcare provider about:
gd_pl6T: 6. The person(s) who can support me
gd_pl6H: Who can encourage or help you? (e.g., family member, friend, healthcare provider, community group)
gd_plTip2B: Write down what works and celebrate your achievements.
gd_plTip3B: Try to include your new habits in your daily schedule.
gd_plTip4B: If you miss a day, start again the next day.
gd_plTip5B: Share your goals with family, friends or your healthcare team.
gd_plEx1: Food: add one serving of vegetables to lunch and dinner.
gd_plEx2: Drinks: replace sugary drinks with water or unsweetened drinks.
gd_plEx3: Activity: walk for 30 minutes, 5 days a week.
gd_plEx4: Habits: avoid alcohol or limit it to a safe level.
gd_plEx5: Health check: get blood tests for liver function, blood sugar, cholesterol and blood pressure as advised by your doctor.
gd_myIntro: There are many misconceptions about liver health. Knowing the facts can help you make safer choices and take better care of your liver.
gd_my1T: Fatty liver happens only to people who drink alcohol.
gd_my1B: Many people think fatty liver is caused only by alcohol.
gd_my1fT: Fatty liver can occur in people who do not drink alcohol.
gd_my1fB: It is common in people who are overweight, have diabetes, high cholesterol or high blood pressure, or follow unhealthy diets.
gd_my2T: If I feel fine, my liver must be healthy.
gd_my2B: Liver disease does not always cause symptoms early on.
gd_my2fT: Liver damage can be present even when you feel well.
gd_my2fB: Many liver conditions, including fatty liver, have no symptoms in the early stages. Regular check-ups can help detect problems early.
gd_my3T: Everyone with fatty liver will develop cirrhosis.
gd_my3B: People worry that fatty liver always leads to serious liver disease.
gd_my3fB: Fatty liver can often be reversed, especially if the underlying causes (such as excess weight, diabetes or heavy alcohol use) are addressed early.
gd_my4T: Only people with obesity develop fatty liver.
gd_my4B: Some believe fatty liver only affects people who are overweight.
gd_my4fT: People with normal weight can also develop fatty liver.
gd_my4fB: It can occur in people with normal weight, including those with diabetes, high cholesterol, a poor diet or a family history.
gd_my5T: A “detox” or herbal remedy can clean my liver.
gd_my5B: Many products claim to “detox” or cure liver problems.
gd_my5fT: There is no proven detox that cleans the liver.
gd_my5fB: The liver already removes harmful substances from the body. Some unregulated supplements can actually harm the liver.
gd_my6T: Exercise only helps if I lose a lot of weight.
gd_my6B: People think exercise is only useful for big weight loss.
gd_my6fT: Physical activity benefits the liver even without major weight loss.
gd_my6fB: Regular activity can reduce liver fat, improve insulin sensitivity, lower cholesterol and support overall liver health, even with small changes in weight.
gd_myKey: Make informed choices based on facts, not myths. If you are concerned about your liver health, talk to your doctor for personalised advice.
gd_fqIntro: Answers to some common questions about fatty liver and liver health. If you have any other questions, please talk to your doctor or healthcare provider.
gd_fqC1B: Yes. Fatty liver can also occur in children, especially those who are overweight, have unhealthy eating habits, or have conditions like diabetes. Early detection and healthy habits can help.
gd_fqC2T: Should a child follow a weight-loss diet?
gd_fqC2B: No. Children should not follow restrictive weight-loss diets. The focus should be on healthy growth, balanced eating and regular physical activity, with guidance from a healthcare provider.
gd_fqC3T: When is a pediatric specialist needed?
gd_fqC3B: A pediatric (child) specialist is needed if a child has persistent liver test abnormalities, suspected fatty liver, other liver conditions, or additional concerns such as obesity, diabetes or abnormal growth.
gd_fqA1B: Yes. In the early stages (fatty liver), it can often improve or even be reversed with lifestyle changes such as healthy eating, regular physical activity, weight management and avoiding alcohol.
gd_fqA2B: Not always. Many people can improve with lifestyle changes alone. Medicines may be advised for selected patients, such as those with MASH or certain associated conditions (e.g., diabetes, high cholesterol).
gd_fqA3T: How often should I be checked?
gd_fqA3B: This depends on your individual risk factors and existing conditions. Your doctor may suggest regular liver tests (liver function tests) and sometimes an ultrasound to monitor your liver health.
gd_fqO1B: Yes. In most cases, regular, safe physical activity (e.g., walking, cycling or light strength exercises) is beneficial, even in older adults. Choose activities appropriate for your fitness level and health conditions.
gd_fqO2B: Yes. Some medicines can affect the liver, especially when used long term or in higher doses. Always take medicines as prescribed and tell your doctor about all your medicines, including over-the-counter products.
gd_fqO3B: Yes. Treatment decisions are individualized. In older adults, choices take into account other health conditions, current medicines, organ function (such as kidney and liver function) and overall tolerability.
gd_fqNoteT: These answers are general; individual medical advice may differ.
gd_fqNoteB: Always talk to your doctor or healthcare provider for advice that is right for your age, health condition and personal circumstances.
gd_5sIntro: Small, consistent actions can make a big difference for your liver at any age. Keep these five simple steps in mind to protect, check and improve your liver health.
gd_5s1B: Be aware of factors that can affect your liver, such as unhealthy weight, diabetes, high cholesterol, high blood pressure, certain medicines and a family history of liver disease.
gd_5s2B: Fatty liver often has no symptoms, especially in the early stages. Taking action early can prevent it from getting worse.
gd_5s3B: Talk to your doctor about liver health checks, especially if you have risk factors or other health conditions.
gd_5s4B: Follow a balanced eating pattern, be physically active, get enough sleep, and avoid tobacco. If you drink alcohol, try to avoid it or keep it low, as advised by your doctor.
gd_5s5B: Liver health is a long-term goal. Small, steady changes — and regular follow-up with your healthcare provider — can make a lasting difference.
gd_5sC3: Get enough sleep for growth and well-being.
gd_5sA1: Choose balanced meals (e.g., more vegetables, whole grains, lean protein).
gd_5sA2: Aim for at least 30 minutes of activity most days.
gd_5sA3: Keep conditions like diabetes, cholesterol and blood pressure under good control.
gd_5sO1: Eat a nutritious, protein-rich diet (e.g., pulses, eggs, soy, dairy).
gd_5sO2: Stay active safely (e.g., walking, light exercises).
gd_5sO3: Keep regular follow-up for liver and other health conditions.
gd_5sKey: A healthier liver supports a healthier you.
gd_hpIntro: Most people can improve their liver health with daily lifestyle changes. However, seek professional support if you are at higher risk, have ongoing concerns, or are advised to do so after a health check.
gd_hpWhenT: It is a good time to seek professional support if you or your family member:
gd_hpWhen1: Have risk factors such as overweight/obesity, diabetes, high cholesterol or high blood pressure.
gd_hpWhen2: Have abnormal liver test results, an ultrasound showing fatty liver, or other ongoing liver concerns.
gd_hpWhen3: Are unsure about the best plan for food, activity, medicines or follow-up.
gd_hpC: See a pediatrician or a pediatric gastroenterology/hepatology service (for liver-related care in children).
gd_hpA: See a primary-care physician, gastroenterologist or hepatologist (for assessment, advice and ongoing care).
gd_hpO: See a primary-care physician or a relevant specialist (e.g., gastroenterologist or hepatologist), with a medication review as needed (to check for possible effects on the liver).
gd_hpKey: Your liver works for you every day. Take care of it.
